implementation_notes: Java expresses absence with java.util.Optional<T>, a value-based container added in Java 8 whose API note is explicit: it is primarily intended as a method return type where 'no result' must be represented and null would be error-prone, and a variable of that type should never itself be null. The compiler does not force the check - get() throws NoSuchElementException and the documentation points to orElseThrow()/orElse() as the preferred exits - and Optional is a final class that cannot be extended, so the classic Maybe structure is replaced by the library type plus map/flatMap/stream composition. Vavr supplies a richer, functional Option for code bases that already use it.
pitfalls: Optional is a value-based class: synchronizing on it or comparing against Optional.empty() with == is wrong (empty() need not be a singleton); use isEmpty()/isPresent().
Optional in fields, parameters and collections multiplies the ways absence can be expressed (null, empty Optional, empty collection); the API note restricts it to return positions.
Optional<Optional<T>> and Optional<List<T>> flatten badly: return an empty collection for 'none of many' and use flatMap instead of nesting wrappers.
get() is a disguised exception - a code base that calls get() everywhere has bought signature noise without safety; orElseThrow() with a meaningful exception is the documented replacement.

variants.name: Vavr Option
variants.implementation_notes: Vavr's Option<T> is the functional alternative: Some/None pattern matching, map/flatMap/getOrElse/orElse, conversions from java.util.Optional and from Try, and value semantics that allow it in fields and collections (unlike the value-based java.util.Optional). Choose it where the code base already uses Vavr's persistent collections and control types and wants one vocabulary for Option/Try/Either; the cost is a third-party dependency tracked against the JDK.
pitfalls: Having both java.util.Optional and Vavr Option in one code base doubles the conversion burden: pick one per layer and convert once at the boundary.
Vavr is a third-party library that must be kept in step with the JDK; its Option is not what most Java reviewers expect in a signature.
